strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks across ExORL and OGBench, with 8 baselines spanning offline RL, representation learning, model-based, contrastive occupancy, and unsupervised RL methods, using 8 seeds (4 for visual tasks) and reporting end-of-fine-tuning performance to avoid evaluation bias.

The paper is well-motivated and clearly positioned: it identifies that prior RL pre-training methods neglect temporal structure and user intention, and situates itself precisely relative to the closest prior work (TD flows of Farebrother et al.) with clear articulation of differences (latent variable intentions vs. FB representations, implicit GPI vs. explicit GPI over a finite intention set).

Thoughtful ablations: the variational intention encoder (vs. HILP/FB intention encodings), the implicit GPI (vs. standard GPI and one-step PI with 44% gain and 8x lower variance), convergence-speed analysis, and extensive hyperparameter sensitivity studies (latent dim, Euler steps, N, expectile, lambda, alpha) in the appendix.

Complete algorithmic detail with pseudocode for pre-training and fine-tuning, full ELBO derivation, information-bottleneck interpretation, and theoretical discussion of implicit GPI convergence in the appendix; open-source implementation released.

Strong results on the most challenging tasks: 20x improvement on jaco over baselines, 36% success-rate improvement on OGBench manipulation, 31% improvement on visual tasks, demonstrating the method scales to pixels and semi-sparse rewards.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: each ingredient is drawn from prior work—flow occupancy models and TD flows from Farebrother et al. [29], expectile losses from IQL, latent intentions from prior variational-intention work (e.g., Ghosh et al., InfoGAIL). The main contribution is the combination plus the implicit GPI scheme, which is relatively incremental for a top-tier venue.

The most important head-to-head comparison—against FB + FOM (essentially TD flows + GPI, the closest baseline)—appears only in the 4-task ablation (Fig. 4), not in the main 40-task benchmark, leaving the central claim (latent intentions beat FB-style intentions) supported on a narrow task set.

InFOM does not dominate uniformly: it underperforms on cheetah walk/walk backward, quadruped run/jump, and several tasks in Table 4, and the claimed 1.8x median improvement is driven largely by a few large-margin domains; per-domain analysis of failures is limited.

Heavy hyperparameter sensitivity: the appendix acknowledges the latent dimension d, KL coefficient lambda, and BC coefficient alpha are crucial and require per-domain (and per-task for visual) tuning, raising reproducibility and practicality concerns and complicating the fair-comparison claim.

Assumption 1 (consecutive transitions share one intention) is a strong structural assumption for heterogeneous multi-user data, and the paper itself admits the consecutive-transition reduction may not capture true intentions; no experiments test robustness when this assumption is violated.

The theoretical justification for implicit GPI (Appendix B.2) is informal and heuristic—convergence to the max over z requires N→infty and mu→1 assumptions that do not hold in practice, and there is no analysis of the bias introduced by the expectile relaxation. Minor errors also reduce polish (e.g., garbled sentence in Sec. 2 related work; Alg. 1 line 7-8 inconsistency between (s − ε) in Eq. 4 and (s − z) in Alg. 1).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks across two established benchmarks (ExORL, OGBench), with eight baselines spanning five categories of pre-training/fine-tuning strategies, 8 random seeds for state-based tasks, and results reported at end of fine-tuning (not cherry-picked peaks).

Thorough ablation studies: the paper isolates the contribution of each component (variational intention encoder vs. HILP/FB intention encodings, implicit GPI vs. standard GPI and one-step PI, flow occupancy models vs. one-step models for convergence speed), plus detailed hyperparameter sensitivity analyses in the appendix.
Good reproducibility: open-source implementation, shared codebase for all baselines, common hyperparameters where possible, and detailed implementation/hyperparameter documentation (Tables 1-3).

Clear technical presentation: the derivation of the ELBO (Appendix B.1) and its information bottleneck interpretation, and the motivation for replacing greedy GPI with expectile-based implicit GPI to avoid backpropagating through the ODE solver, are well reasoned.

Strong results on the most challenging tasks: large gains on OGBench manipulation (36% success rate over best baseline), competitive visual-task performance (31% improvement), and dramatic improvement on ExORL jaco where baselines nearly fail.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the closest prior work (Farebrother et al., TD flows). The core flow-matching occupancy machinery is adopted wholesale; the delta is (1) a variational latent intention encoder over consecutive transitions and (2) expectile-based implicit GPI instead of max over a finite intention set. Both are relatively standard techniques (VAE-style ELBO, IQL-style expectile loss), and the paper's framing as a 'foundation model for RL' overstates the actual contribution.

Headline claims (1.8x median return improvement, 36% success rate increase) are heavily driven by a few outlier domains (e.g., jaco, where baselines make trivial progress). On several ExORL locomotion tasks InFOM actually underperforms simpler baselines (e.g., cheetah walk: 254.8 vs. 443.4 for MBPO+ReBRAC; cheetah run backward is worse than ReBRAC), so the aggregate statistics mask mixed per-task performance.

Assumption 1 (intention consistency across consecutive transitions) is strong and arguably unrealistic: inferring a user intention from a single next state-action pair conflates short-horizon dynamics with long-term intent. The paper acknowledges this only briefly in the limitations and provides no empirical validation that the learned latents correspond to meaningful intentions (no visualization or probing of the latent space).

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: the KL coefficient and BC regularization require per-domain sweeps over wide ranges (e.g., α ∈ {300, 30, 3, 0.3}, with scene/puzzle preferring α=300 while others prefer much smaller values), which weakens the practicality claim and raises concerns about tuning-fairness relative to baselines.

Theoretical support for implicit GPI is thin: Appendix B.2 argues convergence by analogy to expectile properties from Kostrikov et al. rather than a formal analysis for this setting (infinite intentions, finite N samples from a learned generative model with bootstrapped training), leaving the central policy-improvement mechanism empirically but not theoretically grounded.

Writing quality issues, including a garbled sentence in Related Work ('our approach differs in that it does not learn multiple skills during pre-training. in that we also learn a set of latent intentions...') that actually reverses the intended meaning, and other typos that suggest insufficient proofreading.

Ablations of the intention encoder (Fig. 4) use only 4 tasks, and the win is 3/4 with small margins on some, so the evidence that the variational encoder is superior to FB/HILP encodings is not overwhelming.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: pre-training foundation models for RL that capture both temporal (long-horizon) structure and the multi-user, multi-task (intention) structure of large offline datasets. The framing of intentions as latent variables inside an occupancy measure model is clean and well-motivated.

The method is technically coherent: an ELBO-based variational intention encoder is combined with SARSA-style TD flow matching, and fine-tuning uses Monte Carlo Q estimation distilled via an upper expectile loss ('implicit GPI'), which avoids backpropagating through the ODE solver and avoids max over a finite intention set. The connection to the information bottleneck is a nice interpretive bonus.

Evaluation is unusually broad and rigorous for this area: 36 state-based tasks (ExORL + OGBench) plus 4 visual tasks, 8 diverse baselines spanning offline RL, representation learning, model-based, contrastive, and skill-learning categories, multiple seeds, honest reporting (final performance, not best), and strong gains on the hardest manipulation and visual tasks (36% success-rate improvement, 31% over the best baseline on visual tasks).

The ablations are targeted and informative: comparisons to alternative intention encodings (HILP, FB/TD flows), alternative policy extraction (naive GPI, one-step PI), convergence-speed analysis, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies in the appendix.

Reproducibility is strong: full algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter tables shared across methods, domain-specific tuning protocol documented, single-GPU runtimes, and open-source code for the method and all baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental. The core technical ingredients are assembled from prior work: the TD flow occupancy model is taken nearly wholesale from Farebrother et al. [29], and the expectile-based implicit GPI closely mirrors IQL-style expectile regression. The main novel piece is the VAE-style intention encoder over consecutive transitions, which is a fairly standard latent-variable construction (cf. InfoGAIL, latent intentions [34]).

The headline '1.8x median improvement' claim is inflated by the jaco outlier (20x gain) and puzzle/scene tasks; on several ExORL domains (cheetah walk/run-backward, walker stand) InFOM actually underperforms simpler baselines like MBPO+ReBRAC and ReBRAC by wide margins (e.g., 254 vs 447 on cheetah walk). The paper's own Fig. 3 caption admits parity on 7 of 9 domains, which tempers the significance of the aggregate numbers.

The intention representation is coarse: z is inferred from a single next transition (s', a') under Assumption 1, which the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations. There is no direct evidence (e.g., qualitative visualization or probing) that the learned latent z actually corresponds to semantically meaningful user intentions, and no experiments with actual goal-image or language conditioning despite motivating intentions that way.

The method appears hyperparameter-sensitive: domain-specific tuning of the KL coefficient, expectile, BC coefficient, and latent dimension is required (Fig. 7 shows large variance), and per-task tuning for image tasks weakens the 'foundation model' narrative somewhat. Baseline tuning fairness (e.g., for FB+IQL and HILP+IQL) is difficult to verify fully.

Theoretical support is thin: Appendix B.2 offers informal intuition rather than formal guarantees for implicit GPI (relied on 'mild assumptions' from IQL), and no error bounds or analysis of when the consistency assumption fails.

Minor writing issues remain, e.g., the garbled sentence in the offline unsupervised RL related-work paragraph ('differs in that it does not learn multiple skills during pre-training. in that we also learn...'), which suggests incomplete editing.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and important problem: pre-training in RL, where the model must capture both long-horizon temporal structure (occupancy measures) and heterogeneous user intentions latent in the data. Combining variational latent-variable inference with TD-based flow occupancy models is a sensible and novel combination.

The technical formulation is careful and largely sound: the ELBO derivation for the intention encoder (Appendix C.1), its connection to the information bottleneck, and the SARSA variant of the TD flow loss for intention-conditioned occupancy are clearly presented. The implicit GPI via expectile distillation is a clever and practical solution to the instability of differentiating through the ODE solver and the infinite intention space.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks across two standard benchmark suites (ExORL, OGBench), comparison against 8 strong baselines spanning five categories, honest reporting (e.g., acknowledging that InFOM matches but does not beat baselines on 7/9 ExORL domains, and providing a reward-structure analysis for the jaco gap), a real-robotics dataset experiment (RT-1), and thorough ablations (implicit GPI vs. GPI vs. one-step PI, BC regularization, dataset sizes, number of flow samples N, latent dimension, KL and BC coefficients).

Visualization experiments (t-SNE of inferred intentions vs. FB and HILP encodings) provide direct qualitative evidence that the variational encoder recovers meaningful, temporally consistent intentions rather than only improving benchmark numbers.

Reproducibility is strong: open-source JAX implementation, shared codebase for all baselines, full hyperparameter tables including per-domain tuning, modest compute requirements (single A6000, 4–12 hours), and clear evaluation protocols following prior work.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to the closest prior work. The TD flow occupancy model is taken from Farebrother et al. (2025), and the paper's core additions are (1) conditioning on a variational latent intention inferred from consecutive transitions and (2) expectile-based implicit GPI. Each ingredient is a relatively natural extension of well-established components (VAEs, successor features, GPI, expectile losses), so the conceptual leap is moderate.

There is a gap between the theoretical framing and the actual objective: the paper motivates the intention encoder via an ELBO on data likelihood (Eq. 3), but the flow-matching surrogate loss (Eq. 4) is not a likelihood, so the derived ELBO does not strictly justify the implemented objective. The consistency assumption (Assumption 1) that intentions persist across consecutive transitions is strong and only empirically justified; how sensitive the method is to violations of it is not analyzed.

Fine-tuning relies on Monte Carlo estimation of Q from only N=16 sampled future states from the flow model, which the authors themselves acknowledge introduces high variance (reflected in large error bars on several tasks, e.g., cheetah, cube single, puzzle 4x4). This is a notable potential source of instability, and the performance on several harder state-based tasks (cheetah run backward, walker run) is below the best baselines.

The intended connection between inferred latent intentions and downstream tasks is somewhat indirect: during fine-tuning, intentions are sampled from the prior rather than task-conditioned, so the benefit rests entirely on implicit GPI over the latent space; the paper would benefit from more analysis of when/why prior-sampled intentions suffice for a specific downstream task.

Some claims in the abstract/intro (1.8x median return improvement, 36% success rate increase) aggregate over benchmarks where InFOM is often only comparable to strong baselines, so the headline numbers should be interpreted carefully; the paper does hedge this in Sec. 5.1, but the framing could still overstate the generality of the advantage.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a well-motivated problem setting (pre-training on heterogeneous, intention-structured unlabeled datasets) that is meaningfully distinguished from meta-RL and multi-task RL (Appendix B.2).

The technical framework is coherent: a variational intention encoder derived from an ELBO (with a clean information-bottleneck interpretation in Appendix C.1) combined with SARSA-style TD flow occupancy models, and an implicit GPI extraction via expectile distillation that avoids differentiating through the ODE solver.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks across ExORL and OGBench, plus a real-robotics (RT-1 dataset) evaluation, with many baselines reimplemented in a shared codebase, extensive ablations (latent dimension, expectile mu, KL coefficient, BC coefficient, N future states, dataset sizes), and released open-source code.

The qualitative analysis of inferred latent intentions (t-SNE visualizations showing clustering aligned with pick/place phases) provides direct evidence that the variational encoder captures behavioral structure better than Hilbert or forward-backward alternatives.
Honest reporting of negative or mixed results, e.g., parity with baselines on most ExORL domains, sensitivity to sparse rewards on jaco tasks, and hyperparameter sensitivity in Fig. 15.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the closest prior work. The core machinery (SARSA/TD flow occupancy models) is taken directly from Farebrother et al. (2025); the delta amounts to (1) conditioning the flow on a latent inferred from the next transition and (2) replacing max-over-intentions GPI with expectile distillation. Both components are fairly standard tools (VAE-style ELBOs; IQL-style expectile critics), so the contribution reads as a well-executed combination rather than a new idea.

The headline claims (1.8x median return improvement, 36% success-rate improvement) are stronger than what the aggregate figures support. The paper itself concedes InFOM 'performs similarly to, if not better than, prior methods on 7 out of 9 domains'; large gains appear concentrated in a few tasks (jaco, some OGBench manipulation tasks), and the headline statistics appear sensitive to aggregation choices.

The central Assumption 1 (consistency of intentions across consecutive transitions) is strong and largely unexamined: inferring an intention from a single (s', a') pair is a very weak signal, and no experiment stress-tests the method when the assumption is violated (e.g., mixed-intention trajectories, mid-trajectory goal switches) beyond the acknowledged limitation. The stated motivation 'datasets collected by many distinct users' is not validated on the benchmarks used, where datasets come from a single exploration or noisy-expert policy.

The comparison against the most important ablation of the contribution - FB FOM, i.e., TD flows with GPI from Farebrother et al. (2025) - is confined to a small 4-task ablation (Fig. 8) rather than the full benchmark suite, making it hard to judge how much of the gain comes from the intention conditioning versus the flow occupancy backbone.

Performance variability and hyperparameter sensitivity undermine the practical significance: high variance across seeds on several tasks (cheetah walk, cube single, puzzle 4x4), sensitivity to the latent dimension d, and per-task/per-domain tuning of lambda, mu, alpha (Tables 2-3), which weakens reproducibility and the claim of a generally applicable pre-training recipe.

Several design choices appear ad hoc and are justified only empirically: sampling intentions for Q estimation from the KL-divergence-weighted marginal (footnote 3), the MC estimate with N=16 future states (which Fig. 14 shows is insufficient for some tasks), and the asymmetric expectile loss as a 'softmax over intentions' whose theoretical justification is deferred to cited prior work.

The significance of the contribution is bounded: on the easier ExORL domains no method meaningfully improves over simple fine-tuning baselines (IQL/ReBRAC), so the setting where InFOM helps is restricted to a subset of semi-sparse-reward OGBench tasks; the broader claim of a foundation-model-style pre-training framework for RL is not yet supported at that scale.

strengths: The paper combines three ideas (variational latent intention inference, flow-matching occupancy models with TD/SARSA bootstrapping, and implicit GPI via expectile distillation) into a coherent pre-training framework for RL, and the overall design is well-motivated by the long-horizon and heterogeneous-intention challenges of RL foundation models.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 36 state-based tasks from ExORL/DeepMind Control plus 4 image-based OGBench tasks, against 8 baselines spanning five methodological categories, with 8 (4 for visual) random seeds and identical hyperparameters/codespace for all methods.

The ablation and analysis suite is strong: intention-encoder variants (HILP/FB) comparisons, implicit GPI vs. finite-intention GPI vs. one-step PI, BC regularization importance, MC future-state count N, dataset size scaling, and per-hyperparameter sensitivity sweeps in the appendix.

Qualitative analysis (t-SNE visualizations of latent intentions in Figs. 4 & 6) directly supports the central claim that InFOM recovers interpretable, intention-aligned latent structure, distinguishing it from FB/HILP representations.
Reproducibility is excellent: shared codebase in JAX, open-source release, full hyperparameter tables for every method, and modest compute (single A6000, 4–12 hours per experiment).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the occupancy-model backbone is directly inherited from TD flows (Farebrother et al., 2025), the ELBO is a standard VAE/information-bottleneck derivation, and the expectile distillation is adapted from IQL. The contribution is a well-executed combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithm, which limits the paper's ceiling.

The headline aggregate gains mask mixed per-domain results: on ExORL the paper itself concedes InFOM 'performs similarly, if not better' than baselines on 7 of 9 domains, and the 20x improvement on jaco is attributable to sparse-reward pathologies (as the authors' own dense-reward ablation in Fig. 10 shows ReBRAC nearly closes the gap). The clearest wins are confined to the OGBench manipulation suite.

Theoretical support for the core policy-improvement step is thin. Implicit GPI's soundness is discussed only heuristically in Appendix C.2, relying on asymptotic convergence of expectile losses and optimality of the occupancy model; no formal guarantee is given for the actual setting where the flow model is approximate and N is finite, despite the max-over-z objective being acknowledged as unstable.

Assumption 1 (intention consistency) is applied only at the level of consecutive transitions rather than trajectories, which the limitations section admits may not capture the true trajectory-level intentions; the impact of this approximation is studied only qualitatively via t-SNE, not quantitatively.

Practicality concerns: the fine-tuning stage requires N=16 ODE solves (10-step Euler each) per Q estimate every critic update, and performance is sensitive to several tuned coefficients (KL weight, BC coefficient, expectile mu, latent dimension) with domain-specific tuning; the sensitivity analysis in Fig. 15 suggests fragility that could hinder adoption on new domains.
The image-based evaluation is narrow (4 tasks, 4 seeds, all from a single benchmark), so the claim of generality to visual RL rests on limited evidence.
